evidence: src/infrastructure/http/middleware/errorHandler.ts: errorHandler(error, _req, res, _next) is the only place errors become HTTP responses; statusFor(error: DomainError) holds the whole domain-error-to-status mapping (ValidationError→400, NotFoundError→404, InsufficientStockError/InvalidStatusTransitionError→409, otherwise 422).

src/infrastructure/http/middleware/errorHandler.ts: isMalformedJson handles the Express body-parser error (type 'entity.parse.failed') and returns 400 MALFORMED_JSON, which is also part of the HTTP error-response concern.
src/infrastructure/http/middleware/notFoundHandler.ts: notFoundHandler(req, res) returns 404 ROUTE_NOT_FOUND. This is a separate case: a route-level 404, not a domain NotFoundError.
Both files write the same { error: { code, message } } response body inline. This minor repetition could go into a shared helper, but it is not a duplicated business rule.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Both files deal with one concern: the HTTP error-response middleware for the Express app. errorHandler.ts turns thrown errors into HTTP responses: domain errors get mapped status codes, malformed JSON gets 400 and anything else gets 500. notFoundHandler.ts returns a 404 for requests that match no route. createApp.ts registers both as terminal middleware. The status-code mapping lives in one place (statusFor), and neither file bypasses an abstraction the module defines. The only overlap is that every response writes the { error: { code, message } } body inline: three times in errorHandler and once in notFoundHandler. This is a small, stable response format, not duplicated business logic. Pulling it into a shared helper would be a nice refactor, but it isn't the kind of split or duplicated rule the rubric treats as a failure.
